title: No place without God
hook: Hasidic teaching: no place is empty of God

segments.voice: Yesterday, cautions: no magic, no selling holy things, no study without ground beneath it. Your line was study carefully. Whose source did you check? Day one thousand one hundred ninety.

A man is running from his brother. Night falls somewhere in the open, and he lies down on the ground with a stone under his head. Nowhere special. Just the spot where the sun went down. He dreams of a ladder, with angels going up and down it, and when he wakes he says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." The place hadn't changed overnight. Jacob had. Hasidic teachers made much of that surprise. Today's words.
screen: `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.` → `A LADDER IN A DREAM.` → `AND I KNEW IT NOT.`

segments.voice: No place without God. Turn it four ways. First, the prophet. Isaiah sees the angels calling to one another: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory." Not the Temple only. The whole earth. Second, the kabbalists' line. The Tikkunei Zohar, a work in the Zohar's family, says it in Aramaic: leit atar panui minei, there is no place empty of Him. The rabbis even give God a name that means the Place, HaMakom. And remember tzimtzum, a week ago: if God drew in to make room for a world, is that room empty? The Hasidic reading answers no. The hiding is real. The emptiness isn't. Third, the street. Hasidic teachers carried the line out of the study house into kitchens, markets and workshops. If no place is empty of God, then the bus stop, the laundry pile and the waiting room are not outside holiness. They're places where it's hidden. Fourth, the hard places. A line like this is easy at sunset and harder in a bad week. But notice where Jacob found it: on a stone pillow, running for his life. Look back at this week. The vessels broke and the sparks fell. We gathered them and spoke of repairing the world. We followed souls that return and intentions that ride on words, and we learned to study with care. Today it arrives at one simple, demanding line: there is nowhere the sparks fell where God is absent.
screen: `THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL.` · `NO PLACE IS EMPTY OF HIM.` · `THE BUS STOP AND THE LAUNDRY.` · `EVEN ON A STONE PILLOW.` · then, large: `NO PLACE WITHOUT HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find God in one ordinary place. Settle where you are, and breathe. Look at the place you're in right now, exactly as it is: the chair, the light, the sounds, the clutter. Don't tidy it in your mind. Let your eyes move slowly from one ordinary thing to the next. With each one, hold a simple thought: even here. If you pray, you can say Jacob's words quietly: surely the LORD is in this place. If you don't, just stay with the place, and let it be enough. The bell holds the time.
No place without God. The Hasidic teaching, drawn from the Tikkunei Zohar, that no place is empty of Him. Today's words.
Your line: no place without him. Today, in the most ordinary spot you stand, a sink, a sidewalk, a line at the store, say to yourself: even here. Day one thousand one hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Hasidic teachers repeat the line that no place is empty of God as a reason to serve God in ordinary life, at work, at meals and on the road, and not only in the synagogue or study house.

trapdoor: what you thought: God lives in holy places.
what it means: no place is empty of God: not the kitchen, not the bus stop, not the hard day.
what a scholar hears: 'leit atar panui minei' in the Tikkunei Zohar, Isaiah 6:3, and the rabbinic name for God, HaMakom, the Place.
